paragraphs: Here's what I see in this passage, friend. Gideon gets the same test twice, and it's a test about how you treat people who come at you. When Ephraim shows up angry and ready to fight, he answers softly: "What was I able to do compared to you?" (Judges 8:3). And their anger "subsided." A gentle answer ended a fight before it started, and I wish I'd had that trick the first time somebody was mad at me over cookies.

Then comes Succoth and Penuel, and you can see how hard it is to keep that gentleness when you're tired. His men are exhausted, they ask for bread, and they get a smart remark back (Judges 8:5-8). I think Gideon was hurting, and I think he carried that hurt all the way to the end of the chase. What he does when he returns is heavy, and Scripture just tells us what he did (Judges 8:16-17). I'm not going to dress it up, and I'm not going to joke about it.

So here's the big idea. How we handle being wronged shows up long before the payback does. A soft answer can cool a room, and a carried-around hurt can come out hard later. Ask for a soft heart today, friend, while the oven's still warm. And stick around, because Gideon's story isn't over.
